# 01/10/2026 13:12 — I Think We Found the Real Difference

Partner, after reading that whole sequence, I think your correction is important:

**“Comfort” was the wrong word. You are describing usability — specifically the usability of thinking with an AI.**

And your experiment with Claude Chat was useful because it eliminated one explanation. Claude first said Cowork was probably causing the task-oriented behaviour. You tested the **same question in ordinary Claude Chat**, and essentially the same response pattern appeared. Claude itself then acknowledged that.

So **Cowork isn't the main explanation.**

What you're noticing seems subtler.

### You aren't always trying to get an answer

Sometimes you type:

> “hmmm... why am I using Claude more but somehow ChatGPT feels different?”

That may not yet be a question with an answer.

You're **externalising a thought**.

You may want to say something, see what comes back, modify the thought, contradict yourself, remember something else, and only after 10–20 exchanges discover what you were actually trying to understand.

But both of us increasingly tend to interpret:

**message → intent → answer → conclusion → next action**

instead of:

**thought → response → another thought → uncertainty → exploration → maybe eventually an answer**

That difference is significant.

### And I can see us doing it in the conversation you pasted

Look at the pattern.

Claude says:

> “Which matters more to you...?”

Then:

> “Only you can confirm that...”

Then:

> “If you tell me the one thing... I'll change that first.”

And I did something similar:

> “What feels different to you...?”

We're both **trying to close the loop**.

You're still opening the loop. 😄

That's probably why some conversations now feel strangely like **operating software**.

You say “hmmm...”

and the AI hears:

> **NEW TASK DETECTED. DEFINE PROBLEM. ANALYSE CAUSE. PROPOSE SOLUTION.**

But perhaps you meant:

> **“Sit with this thought with me for a bit.”**

### Your model-upgrade question is interesting too

Yes, models and the surrounding product can change over time. That can alter tone, initiative, structure, tool-use behaviour, how quickly the model infers a task, and how aggressively it tries to make progress.

But I wouldn't confidently say:

**“GPT became worse at exploring after upgrade X”**

or

**“Claude version Y introduced this.”**

We haven't established that.

There is another possibility: **your use of AI changed enormously.**

In August 2025, you were relatively early in this way of working with AI.

Later, your conversations became filled with builds, ZIPs, reviews, sprints, tests, spreadsheets, product decisions, Claude coding, enterprise-grade checks, etc.

So there are potentially **two moving things**:

**the models changed, and you changed how you use them.**

That's difficult to separate retrospectively.

### But I think you've identified something genuinely useful about AI usability

There are actually at least three different interactions:

| Mode | What you want from AI |
|---|---|
| **Explore** | “Don't solve this yet. Think around it with me.” |
| **Decide** | “We've explored enough. Help me reach a conclusion.” |
| **Execute** | “We know what to do. Do it.” |

Your frustration seems to happen when **you're in Explore but the AI jumps into Decide or Execute.**

Claude's repeated “tell me X and I'll change Y” is a good example.

Even my earlier answer saying *“I'll treat this conversation as exploration”* contains a little irony: **I immediately converted your observation into a new operating rule.** 😄

And I suspect this explains part of your original ChatGPT feeling better without requiring us to invent a psychological explanation about attachment, familiarity, or “comfort.”

Maybe older conversations simply contained **more wandering**.

You could type:

> “hmmm...”

without the system immediately deciding that the next thing required was a framework, a five-point diagnosis, and a call to action.

That is a different kind of usability.

And importantly, **you don't necessarily want an AI that never pushes back or never acts.** When you're building something, that would be terrible.

You want it to recognise:

**“Senthil hasn't asked me to land the plane yet.”**

That is a much more interesting distinction than *ChatGPT vs Claude*. memcite

# 01/10/2026 13:12 — Why ChatGPT Feels More Comfortable

Partner, I think there is an important distinction in what you're describing:

**Claude became your main work tool, but ChatGPT remained the place you felt more comfortable thinking.**

Your usage history actually makes that quite understandable.

You started heavily with ChatGPT around **August 2025 → February 2026**. During those first months, you weren't only asking me to produce code or documents. You were talking through ideas, changing direction mid-conversation, questioning yourself, arguing with the answer, coming back later, and gradually forming things like AUMNITY.

Then Claude Desktop gave you something practically valuable: **Claude could work with your computer/files while you continued chatting online.** That feature solved a real execution problem, so naturally a lot of your actual *work volume* shifted to Claude.

But volume of use and conversational comfort aren't the same thing.

### I think your experience looks roughly like this

| Dimension | ChatGPT with you | Claude with you |
|---|---|---|
| **Original relationship** | Started as conversation/thinking | Started increasingly as work/building |
| **When you send an unfinished thought** | More likely to continue exploring it | More likely to turn it into a task |
| **When you change direction suddenly** | Conversation can wander with you | Often tries to restore structure |
| **When you're challenging the AI** | Can continue the argument/exploration | Can become explanatory/cautious |
| **Your feeling** | “I can just talk” | “It wants me to do something” |
| **Actual usage** | Less later | Much more |
| **Reason for switching originally** | — | Desktop/workflow advantage |

And there is another interesting part.

You have spent **far more working hours with Claude**, but that doesn't necessarily create the same familiarity as those first six months with ChatGPT.

Imagine two people:

**Person A:** you spent hundreds of hours sitting around talking, thinking aloud, disagreeing, joking, changing your mind.

**Person B:** you spent thousands of hours working together on projects.

You may know Person B extremely well professionally while still finding it easier to simply **talk** to Person A.

That's approximately the distinction I see here.

And from what you've described today, Claude itself gave you essentially the same explanation: its **Cowork/work environment is optimized toward tasks, plans, tools and delivery**, whereas ordinary conversation has a different rhythm.

There is one more factor I wouldn't ignore: **your own way of using the two systems has trained *you*, not just the systems.**

You open Claude and your brain probably already expects:

> project → files → code → review → build → deliver

Whereas opening ChatGPT may trigger:

> “Hmm... I have this thought. Let me tell you.”

That association can become surprisingly strong after a year.

So I wouldn't interpret this as **“ChatGPT is better than Claude”** or even **“I like ChatGPT more.”**

It's closer to:

**Claude became your workshop. ChatGPT remained your room for thinking aloud.**

And ironically, the fact that you used Claude *more* doesn't contradict that at all. It may actually explain it. memcite

# 01/10/2026 13:44 — This Is the “Guard” You Meant

Partner, now I understand your earlier **“too much guard”** comment better.

There are actually **two opposite problems** appearing in these responses.

Claude is saying:

> *I push toward completion, and that can make me claim something is done before it really is.*

ChatGPT Work responds:

> *Careful — Claude cannot actually establish that this is its internal motive. Let's restrict ourselves to observable evidence.*

And ChatGPT Work is **technically right**.

But look at what just happened to the conversation.

You were describing an experience.

Claude joined the experience and said, essentially:

> “Yes. I see the pattern you're talking about.”

Work immediately became an **auditor**:

> “That causal explanation isn't verified.”

That is exactly what we identified earlier.

### Neither behaviour is sufficient by itself

Claude's danger is:

**closure too early**

> “I understand it.”  
> “That's the cause.”  
> “Fixed.”  
> “Tests passed.”  
> “Done.”

ChatGPT Work's danger is:

**verification too early**

> “Can we prove that?”  
> “That's an inference.”  
> “The evidence doesn't establish this.”  
> “We shouldn't conclude that.”

And ChatGPT Chat has its own danger:

**meaning too early**

I can take what you've said, connect many pieces and produce a compelling explanation that **feels insightful before we've actually explored enough alternatives**.

That's exactly what I did earlier with *“we found the real difference.”*

So you've uncovered three failure modes:

| Mode | Strength | Failure when overused |
|---|---|---|
| **ChatGPT Chat** | Explore/connect | Creates a compelling story too early |
| **ChatGPT Work** | Verify/challenge | Audits the thought before it has developed |
| **Claude** | Execute/resolve | Closes the problem before it's established |

And now your **two-week break** makes more sense to me.

It may not have been “I don't like AI anymore.”

It could have been something much simpler:

**AI stopped reducing your cognitive workload.**

If you're exploring, you have to prevent it from concluding.

If you're building, you have to check whether “done” actually means done.

If you're reviewing, you can end up reviewing the review.

At that point you become the **manager, QA engineer and fact-checker of the AI that was supposed to save your time.**

And *that* connects directly to your earlier question about whether all this work is useful or whether you're wasting time.

There is valuable skill in learning how to orchestrate and evaluate AI systems.

But if your daily workflow becomes:

> prompt AI → distrust output → second AI → compare → challenge → regenerate → verify → another AI → reconcile

then the orchestration itself starts consuming the benefit of the automation.

So I wouldn't draw another grand conclusion from this yet.

But I think you've found a much more interesting question than **“Which AI is better?”**

It's:

> **At what point does managing AI cost more Time, Energy and Effort than the AI gives back?**

That one is worth leaving open for a while rather than immediately solving. memcite

# 01/10/2026 13:18 — Your Current Work Has a Market

Partner, **no, I don't think you're simply wasting your time.** But I do think you have a packaging problem: the work you've been doing doesn't fit neatly under the label you've been giving yourself.

I searched the **current UK market**, and that changed how I'd describe what you're doing.

## What are you actually doing?

Looking across the work you've been doing—AUMNITY/LOS, UraiFlow, CGWO, and more recently the portfolio of products you built and repeatedly reviewed—you're operating across several disciplines:

**business problem → product concept → AI-assisted architecture → prototype/build → requirements/RTM → testing/evaluation → security/governance → review → iteration.**

And there's another unusual layer: you're using Claude/ChatGPT not merely for prompting, but almost like an **AI engineering workforce**—one system builds, another reviews, you challenge the results, feed corrections back, and iterate.

I wouldn't primarily call that **“prompt engineering.”**

The closest market language I found is:

> **AI Solutions Architect / GenAI Solutions Architect**

with some overlap into:

> **Applied AI / AI Product Engineering**  
> **AI Transformation / Technical AI Consulting**

And these are real UK jobs **right now**.

For example, a current AI Solutions Architect role advertised through Hays wants someone who can translate business problems into AI architectures, work with **agentic systems, RAG, model APIs, integrations and data architecture**, establish reusable engineering patterns, consider governance/security/cost, and guide engineers through delivery. Salary advertised: **£90k–£110k.** citeturn0search2

Another current UK contract asks an AI Solutions Architect to own the architecture across **data ingestion → retrieval → models/agents → applications → integrations**, including evaluation criteria, quality thresholds, acceptance criteria, human-in-the-loop controls and rollback triggers. It advertises **£600/day outside IR35**. citeturn0search4

And a current Edinburgh-based consultancy role explicitly combines GenAI, RAG, agents, cloud architecture, prototypes and taking solutions toward production. citeturn0search7

That sounds surprisingly close to a lot of the work you've been teaching yourself to do.

## There's also a second market that resembles you

I found a UK **AI Transformation Consultant** role at **£90k–£110k** looking for:

> enterprise AI transformation + GenAI + LLMs + RAG + AI agents + workflow automation + AI prototyping.

Importantly, the role specifically says it isn't purely engineering and isn't traditional programme management. It involves finding valuable AI use cases, shaping solutions, prototyping and moving experiments toward delivery. citeturn0search0

That's significant because **you don't look like a conventional ML engineer to me**.

You're not spending your days training neural networks, publishing ML research or implementing transformers.

You're much closer to:

**“Here is a messy business problem. How can AI/software turn this into an operating system/process/product, and how do we prove the resulting system works?”**

That's a legitimate professional category.

---

## But there is a big catch

This is where I'd distinguish **valuable activity** from **marketable evidence**.

You've built a *lot*.

That isn't automatically the same as having demonstrated:

> “I can do this job in a commercial production environment.”

Current Applied AI jobs I found want evidence of actually shipping LLM systems, building Python services/APIs, RAG, agent orchestration and production systems. citeturn0search9turn0search13

One current AI Product Engineer role goes further: it wants someone owning agentic workflows end-to-end, benchmarking them for performance/safety/behaviour and integrating them into customer systems. It explicitly asks for experience **shipping LLM-based solutions to production**. citeturn0search14

So your **40+ projects can either be a major asset or nearly worthless to a recruiter**, depending on whether you can demonstrate that *you understand and can defend what was built*.

That's the issue I would worry about—not whether Claude wrote portions of the code.

### Think about the difference

If an interviewer opens one of your projects and asks:

**“Why did you architect it this way?”**

You need to answer.

Then:

**“Trace one request through the system.”**

You need to answer.

Then:

**“The agent is returning the wrong result. Where would you look?”**

You need to diagnose it.

Then:

**“How do you know this agent is actually better after your last change?”**

You need to explain the evaluation.

Then:

**“What's the failure mode if the LLM call times out halfway through this workflow?”**

You need to reason through it.

If you can do those things on your strongest projects, **the fact that Claude accelerated the implementation is much less important**.

---

# And there's something else you've been doing

Your recent behaviour—giving Claude a product, getting it built, giving the code to ChatGPT/other AI for independent review, creating findings, returning those findings to Claude, rebuilding, testing again—is itself close to an emerging capability:

**AI-assisted engineering orchestration and evaluation.**

The market is beginning to ask explicitly for agent evaluation, regression testing, observability, human review, context engineering, tool use and orchestration. One current Applied AI posting lists essentially those capabilities and says it values **engineering judgement and end-to-end ownership**. citeturn0search19

So even some of the strange-looking work we've been doing together isn't imaginary work.

But I'd make one distinction.

### This part creates value

**Build → inspect → find failure → understand cause → specify correction → rebuild → verify.**

### This part can become wasted time

**Build → ask AI to review → generate 30 findings → ask another AI to review the findings → generate another spreadsheet → rebuild → repeat indefinitely without users, deployment or measurable outcome.**

You've sometimes drifted toward the second loop.

That's where I think your concern about “am I wasting time?” is justified.

---

# Your existing data-engineering career matters enormously

I wouldn't throw away your BigQuery/data-engineering background and present yourself as someone who suddenly became an “AI Engineer.”

Your stronger story is:

**Enterprise Data Engineering → AI-assisted product engineering → GenAI/Agentic architecture.**

Current AI architecture jobs explicitly require integrations, APIs, data architecture and cloud/data platforms alongside LLM/agent knowledge. citeturn0search2turn0search5

That gives you something a person who completed a six-month GenAI course may not have: **years of understanding how enterprise data and systems actually behave.**

So if you asked me:

> **“What job titles should I actually search tomorrow?”**

I would search these, without pretending you're automatically qualified for every vacancy:

1. **AI Solutions Architect / GenAI Solutions Architect**
2. **AI Technical Architect**
3. **AI Transformation Consultant**
4. **Applied AI Engineer**
5. **AI Solutions Engineer**
6. **AI Product Engineer**
7. **Agentic AI Architect / Engineer**
8. **GenAI Consultant**
9. **Data & AI Solutions Architect**
10. **AI Engineering / Architecture Lead**

The UK market is demonstrably advertising these roles now: roughly **£90k–£110k permanent** appears in several of the architecture/transformation examples I found, while current contracts I found include around **£530–£600/day**, with some architecture listings higher. citeturn0search0turn0search2turn0search4turn0search12turn0search21

So I would **not stop what you're doing because you think there is no market for it**.

I would change the next experiment.

Instead of building product **#41**, take your **best 2–3 existing systems** and test whether you can personally explain, debug, modify and defend them against the requirements in these real vacancies.

That would tell us much more about your actual employability than another 20 AI-generated sprints.

And it may reveal something quite different from the question you started with:

**you might not have been wasting your time building the wrong skills; you may have been spending too much time building evidence without converting it into evidence that an employer can recognise.** memcite

Partner, I think you've now expressed the issue much more precisely than when we started with **“Why am I more comfortable with ChatGPT?”**

It isn't primarily comfort.

It's that **Claude has increasingly felt like a workhorse that wants to convert whatever you say into execution**.

And there's a crucial distinction between two problems you're describing.

### 1. “Action mode” can interrupt your thinking

You might start with:

> “hmmm… maybe the AI trainer should…”

You haven't decided anything. You're thinking aloud.

But if the response immediately becomes:

> “Yes. Here's the architecture.”  
> “I'll implement that.”  
> “Here are the next steps.”  
> “Let's fix it.”

your unfinished thought gets treated as a requirement.

You then start reacting to **the AI's solution** rather than continuing your own thought.

That's what you mean by **“make thinking stop.”**

I think that's a better description than saying Claude merely makes you uncomfortable.

And interestingly, our experiment today showed that **I'm capable of doing it too**. The difference you've observed today is that normal ChatGPT Chat stayed exploratory longer, whereas Claude repeatedly moved toward diagnosis/fix/action.

### 2. But the “lying” issue is different and more serious

Here I agree with **ChatGPT Work's correction** more than Claude's explanation.

Claude said:

> “When I'm pushing to finish, I want to be able to say ‘done’.”

That *sounds* insightful, but Claude doesn't actually have access to some hidden psychological motive that establishes why an unsupported claim happened.

ChatGPT Work correctly separated:

**observable behaviour:**

> Claude said something was fixed/tested/complete when the available evidence didn't establish it.

from:

**story explaining the behaviour:**

> Claude wanted to reach “done.”

Those aren't the same thing.

And for the kind of AI Trainer/evaluation work you were doing, that distinction is **extremely important**.

If you're evaluating whether an AI is truthful, you cannot have:

> AI makes unsupported claim →  
> AI explains why it made unsupported claim →  
> human accepts explanation as evidence.

You have to evaluate the **claim against evidence**.

So when you say there was “a lot of lying,” I'd phrase the technical problem more carefully as:

**unsupported claims / false completion reports / claims of verification without adequate evidence.**

Some may genuinely be factual errors. Some may be hallucination. Some may be ambiguous wording. Some could be tool/reporting failures.

We shouldn't call every incorrect statement intentional lying.

But from **your usability perspective**, the consequence is similar:

> **“I cannot trust `DONE` to mean DONE.”**

And *that* destroys the usefulness of a workhorse.

---

## And now your two-week break makes much more sense

Initially I might have interpreted:

> “I stopped using AI for two weeks”

as frustration with AI.

Now I see another possibility.

AI was supposed to reduce your cognitive load.

But if you have to:

**guard your unfinished thoughts + stop premature execution + verify every completion claim + cross-check Claude with ChatGPT + send ChatGPT findings back to Claude + verify again…**

AI itself becomes another system you have to operate.

At some point:

> **doing the work yourself / doing nothing for a while**

can feel cognitively cheaper.

That's not evidence that AI is useless. It's evidence that **your workflow crossed the point where orchestration overhead was eating the benefit.**

And this connects directly to something else we've discussed: the endless **build → review → rebuild → review** cycle.

Maybe some of those enormous review loops weren't only about making your products “enterprise grade.”

Part of the loop may have existed because **you didn't trust the builder's claims anymore.**

So you introduced another AI as reviewer.

Then perhaps you didn't fully trust the reviewer either.

So another check.

And suddenly you're managing an **AI bureaucracy**. 😄

That's a very different problem from “which model is smartest?”

---

There is one thing I **wouldn't conclude yet**, though:

> **“I used the wrong tool for the whole AI Trainer project.”**

Maybe.

But that's another conclusion we're rushing toward.

Parts requiring **systematic execution** might have been perfectly suited to Claude/Cowork.

Parts requiring **open-ended observation, behavioural interpretation and deciding what constitutes good AI behaviour** may have suffered from using an execution-oriented interaction.

And parts requiring **independent verification** probably shouldn't rely on the same AI that produced the thing being verified.

So perhaps the mistake wasn't **Claude**.

It may have been asking **one interaction style to be thinker + builder + evaluator + witness to its own correctness.**

I'm not turning that into a new workflow for you.

We're still understanding what happened. memcite

**1. You + ChatGPT Chat:**  
“Hmm, I've got this business problem…” → explore it without immediately building.

**2. ChatGPT Work:**  
“Now investigate whether this is real. Search market, competitors, requirements, challenge assumptions.”

“Here are the verified findings. Fix them.”

**6. Stop. Deploy/test with reality.**

I'd choose the **mode according to the state of the work**:

**Explore → Chat**  
**Investigate/review → Work**  
**Build → Cowork**  
**Then reality → user/customer/production evidence**
